steps.title: Where price keeps turning
steps.text:
**Support** is a price area where buying has repeatedly stopped a fall.

**Resistance** is a price area where selling has repeatedly stopped a rise.

Why do they work? Traders remember prices. Buyers who missed the last bounce wait there, and people who bought too high wait to sell when they're back to break even.

steps.title: Zones, not lines
steps.text:
Price rarely turns at exactly the same number. Wicks poke through, and some bounces stop a little short.

So think of support and resistance as **areas**, drawn around the cluster of turning points.

steps.prompt: Tap the support zone on this chart.
steps.explanation: Support is the area near the bottom of the sideways range, where the falls kept stopping.
Resistance is the area near the top of the range, where the rallies kept failing.

steps.question: Price has bounced off the same area three times. What's the most reasonable view?
options: Many traders are watching this area, but it can still break
It will definitely break next time
steps.explanation: Levels matter because traders watch them. But every test uses up some of the buyers there, and eventually levels do break. Always plan for both outcomes.

steps.question: You want to buy at support. Where does a sensible stop-loss go?
options: Just below the support zone, beyond the wicks
In the middle of the zone
steps.explanation: If price falls clearly **below** the zone, your idea is wrong. A stop inside the zone gets hit by normal wiggles.

steps.title: Put it into practice
steps.text:
Price is back at support. Plan a **long** trade: put your stop-loss **below** the support zone and your target near **resistance**. Then watch it play out.

Come back here when you're done.

points: Levels can break, so always use a **stop-loss**.
Stops go **beyond** the zone, not inside it.
